resources.string: Everyone gets a lane and a big pad in their own zone, and everybody plays at the same time. Use as many fingers as you like.
Sprint: when the countdown ends, tap your pad as fast as you can. First to fill the track wins the round. Tapping before GO freezes your pad for a moment.
Rhythm: a ring shrinks onto your pad. Tap just as it lands. Perfect and good taps move you on; early, late and extra taps set you back.
Mash and Brake: tap fast on green, slow down on amber, and take your hands off on red. A tap on red costs ground and freezes your pad.

Computers fill empty lanes. Choose Relaxed tapping or Hold to tap in the setup if fast tapping is hard: the target is smaller, the windows wider, and a held pad taps for you. Same screen only: there is no Nearby or Online mode.
Drumming tests of tapping speed find most people top out at around six to eight taps a second with one finger, which is why this game limits each finger.
Two to four people pull one marker, each from their own pad, all at once. Teams pull along a rope; in a free-for-all the marker is pulled toward everyone\'s corner.
Tap your pad to pull the marker toward your line. Bring it over the line to win the round, and win most rounds to win the match.
Every pull costs stamina, and a pull is only as strong as the stamina behind it. Mash the pad and you run dry in about two seconds.
Hold a finger down to rest and charge up, then let go for a heave that pulls up to four times harder. Hold, release, tap, repeat.

Uneven teams pull in proportion, so a lone player is stronger against three. Computers fill empty pads. Relaxed pulling and Hold to pull help if fast tapping is hard. Same screen only: there is no Nearby or Online mode.
Tug of war was an Olympic event from 1900 to 1920, and the winning team in 1908 was a team of London police officers.
